entries.topic: The family partnership and the founder's will: private by design

claims.text: On 27 September 1810 Mayer Amschel Rothschild and three sons (Amschel, Salomon, Carl/Callmann) signed the first partnership agreement, 'Mayer Amschel Rothschild & Sons'; James, under age, was to join on majority; Nathan, already in London, was not a party. Term: ten years, renewable. Five signed and sealed copies were made.

Capital under the 1810 agreement (gulden): Mayer Amschel 370,000; Amschel 185,000; Salomon 185,000; Carl 30,000; James 30,000 (held without interest until majority). Profit shares out of 50 parts: Mayer Amschel 25, Amschel 12, Salomon 12. Partners waived interest on their capital.

The 1810 agreement shut the books to heirs: heirs of a dead partner could not demand to see the books, had to accept the last balance sheet, and were paid their share in company stock, not cash. Inventory and balance sheets were to be drawn up only 'as soon as business affairs permit' (Archive's summary, approximate wording).

Under the 1810 agreement no partner could do business or trade on the Stock Exchange without the others' prior knowledge; disputes went to Mayer Amschel as arbitrator, or after his death to two arbitrators and a chairman — i.e. to private arbitration, not to court. A breach penalty of 20,000 thalers was payable within 24 hours.

The Archive states that partners were male family members only; women advised and used their social connections but could not formally join, so that sons-in-law could not claim a controlling interest.

Mayer Amschel died on 19 September 1812. History Today summarises his will as laying down that only his sons should own the business; his daughters and their husbands and children were excluded. A 2022 review of Natalie Livingstone's The Women of Rothschild says the will explicitly forbade female descendants (daughters and the wives of male descendants) from holding shares or having a say.

A Publishers Weekly review of Ferguson's first volume describes 'a mandated unity' that excluded 'daughters, in-laws and strangers'; Skidelsky's review of Ferguson says Mayer Amschel's insistence on a family partnership was 'law for a century'. Of 21 marriages involving his descendants between 1824 and 1877, 15 were between direct descendants (Skidelsky summarising Ferguson).

Later agreements exist but their terms were not found online: the Archive's 2002 acquisitions list records 'Family partnership agreements, 1815-1862' and 'Balance sheets, 1828-1910'; the London house page says Lionel modified the Partnership Agreement in 1838 'to retain the relative autonomy of the London house'. Richard Cooper's review of Ferguson says the firm stayed a transnational partnership for five generations through family loyalty, written agreements and intermarriage.

Nathan Mayer Rothschild's own will (drawn up in his last days, July 1836) told his four sons to co-operate with their mother Hannah and not to engage in 'any transactions of moment' without first asking her 'maternal advice' (quoted by the Archive).

NOT ESTABLISHED: that Mayer Amschel's 1812 will forbade any public inventory of the estate, barred lawsuits, or ordered the eldest son of the eldest son to head the family. No Archive page, review of Ferguson, or reference work fetched states these provisions. Treat them as unverified popular lore until checked in Ferguson vol. 1 or Elon's Founder.

entries.topic: Private communication: Judendeutsch letters, couriers and the archive

claims.text: The brothers wrote to each other in Judendeutsch, which the Archive defines as German written in Hebrew characters. The Archive says it was 'not in itself a code' but was hard to decipher, and so protected the letters 'from prying eyes'.

The Archive holds about 20,000 brothers' letters (1811-1868) in about 142 boxes; 'no precise assessment' of the number has been made. James, the last surviving brother from 1861, wrote in Judendeutsch to his London nephews until his death in 1868. Transcription began in 1989 (mainly by Mordechai Zucker); about 2,500 letters had been fully translated by c.2000.
The Archive's 'Breaking the seal' states: 'There is a break in the letters from 1818 to 1825 for reasons which are not clear'; accidental destruction is the likeliest explanation offered.

'Breaking the seal' says letters went almost daily, to keep up the co-operation set out in the partnership agreements, and that the family's couriers gave swifter delivery of information than almost anyone else in Europe. It mentions 'private code names' but gives no examples.

Spear's magazine mentions 'family nicknames and codes indecipherable to outsiders' and couriers, pigeons and chartered boats, but gives no examples or source; its claim that envelope colour signalled sterling's direction is unsourced.

The Rothschild Archive in London was established in 1978 by Victor, 3rd Lord Rothschild, and passed to The Rothschild Archive Trust in 1999. Ferguson had free access to all files except the last thirty years, with no censorship (per Steinberg's LRB review); 'Breaking the seal' (2000) notes only a few historians had used the Judendeutsch letters.

A separate family archive, founded by Salomon in Frankfurt in 1844 and moved to Vienna in 1927, was seized after the Anschluss (inventory 2 April 1938), sent to a Gestapo store in Berlin, ended up in the Red Army's Special Archive in Moscow (from spring 1945; opened 1990), and was returned to the Viennese branch's descendants in 2001.
NOT ESTABLISHED: any specific code name (for a person or state) used in the letters. No fetched source gives an example.

entries.topic: How big: combined capital of the houses (Ferguson's figures)

claims.text: Ferguson (as summarised by Skidelsky): capital grew from £10,000 in 1797 to £1.77 million in 1818. Ferguson's The Ascent of Money (2008, p. 88, cited by Wikipedia) rounds the 1818 figure to £1.8 million for the combined capital of the five houses.

1825: per Ferguson (The Ascent of Money, via Wikipedia), combined capital was about nine times that of Baring Brothers and the Banque de France; Steinberg's LRB review of Ferguson says the combined assets of the five houses were nine times the capital of Barings.
1844: £7.78 million, 'ten times that of their chief rivals, the Baring brothers' (Skidelsky summarising Ferguson).
1852: £9.5 million combined (Ferguson, The Ascent of Money, via Wikipedia).

1862: £22 million combined; 1874: £34 million combined, after which capital growth largely stopped, partly because profits were drawn for family spending (Skidelsky summarising Ferguson). Skidelsky calls 1852-1874 Ferguson's 'golden age'.
1899: £41 million combined, more than the five largest German joint-stock banks together (Ferguson, The Ascent of Money, via Wikipedia).

Return on capital at the London house fell from 9.8% (1870-79) to 3.9% (1900-09), while Barings earned 27.1% in 1900-09 (Skidelsky summarising Ferguson). Steinberg: for most of the 19th century the Rothschilds were 'the biggest bank in the world by a wide margin'.

Personal fortunes, per Ferguson: Nathan's net worth at death (1836) equalled 0.62% of British national income (The Ascent of Money, via Wikipedia); James's fortune at death (1868) was just over 4% of French GDP (Skidelsky; Skidelsky's '$50 billion' modern equivalent is his own and he notes Ferguson's is lower).
NOT ESTABLISHED: combined capital figures for 1815 and 1828 (e.g. the often-repeated £4.3 million for 1828). Not found in any fetched source.

entries.topic: How long the London house stayed a private partnership

claims.text: N M Rothschild & Sons ceased to be a partnership and became a limited company, N M Rothschild & Sons Limited, on 30 September 1970 (Archive).

Steps before that: 1838, Lionel modified the partnership agreement to keep the London house's autonomy; 1941, Rothschilds Continuation Ltd formed as a corporate partner to ensure continuity in wartime; 1960, first non-family partner admitted (Archive).

In 1915 the London house still used single-entry bookkeeping and had 'only one typewriter' (Skidelsky summarising Ferguson). Skidelsky also says 'the partnership system ended in 1905' — unclear what this refers to; it conflicts with the Archive's 1970 date for London and should not be used without checking Ferguson.
The Paris house, de Rothschild Frères, became Banque Rothschild, a limited-liability company, in 1967/1 January 1968 (the Archive and Wikipedia give both dates).

entries.topic: Wealth in land, houses, vineyards and art

claims.text: Nathaniel de Rothschild bought Château Brane-Mouton in 1853 and renamed it Château Mouton Rothschild; Wikipedia gives the price as 1,175,000 francs, from the Paris banker Thuret.

Château Lafite was bought at a Paris auction on 8 August 1868 by agents of Baron James de Rothschild for 4,140,000 francs (plus 300,000 francs for the Carruades estate). James died on 15 November 1868 'never having set foot on the property'.

Ferdinand de Rothschild bought the c.2,700-acre Waddesdon estate from the Duke of Marlborough in 1874 for about £200,000; the house was built 1874-1885 (foundation stone 1877, first house party 1883, west extension 1889), architect Hippolyte Destailleur. The Archive's timeline gives completion as 1884.

James de Rothschild bequeathed Waddesdon, its main collections and grounds to the National Trust in 1957; it opened to the public in 1959. Ferdinand's Renaissance collection went separately to the British Museum as the Waddesdon Bequest. (The Archive timeline's wording credits Dorothy de Rothschild with the 1957 gift; Waddesdon's own page says James bequeathed it and Dorothy chaired the management committee until 1988.)
Mentmore was designed by Joseph Paxton for Mayer de Rothschild (timeline entry 1851); it passed to the Rosebery family and was sold in 1977.
James de Rothschild began the Château de Ferrières in 1853 (built 1853-1859); Guy and Marie-Hélène de Rothschild gave it to the University of Paris in 1975.
Skidelsky (summarising Ferguson) says capital growth stalled after 1874 partly because profits were withdrawn for family spending — the link between the houses and the stalled capital.

entries.topic: Dispersion and loss of the houses

claims.text: Naples: C M de Rothschild e figli was founded by Carl in 1821 and stopped trading in 1863, after Garibaldi took Naples (September 1860); Adolphe Carl would not work with the new regime and left the partnership, and the other houses would not back the deposed Francis II.

Frankfurt: after the death of Wilhelm Carl, the last partner, in 1901 the family voluntarily liquidated M A Rothschild & Söhne, with no male heir and no family member willing to move to Frankfurt; the remaining business went to the Disconto-Gesellschaft of Berlin. The Naples records were destroyed in that 1901 liquidation.

Vienna: the Archive says the Vienna house closed in March 1938. Louis von Rothschild was arrested after the Anschluss (at Aspern airport, per the Archive's biography), imprisoned and then held at the Hotel Metropole, and released in July 1939 after family negotiations and a payment the Archive gives as $21,000,000. His assets were put under a German commissioner.

JTA reported on 14 May 1939 that Louis had reached Switzerland and that he had been held 'until he made good the losses of the Kredit Anstalt'. This conflicts with the Archive's July 1939 release date.

S M von Rothschild was placed under compulsory administration in March 1939 and, per Wikipedia (citation-needed tag), sold in October 1939 to Merck, Finck & Co and renamed E. v. Nicolai & Co. The Archive says only that the business 'was sold and effectively wound up'.

The Austrian Commission for Provenance Research (2013) records that immediately after the Anschluss the Nazi authorities moved to expropriate the Viennese branch's assets, and ruled the archive's confiscation null and void under the 1946 Nullity Act.

Paris: Banque Rothschild was one of 39 banks compulsorily nationalised by the Mitterrand government; the Archive and Wikipedia date the nationalisation to 1982 (the Archive also writes 1981-82). It was renamed Compagnie Européenne de Banque, and Wikipedia says the state paid the family 150 million francs. The family restarted as P.O. Gestion in 1983 and regained use of its name in October 1986.

Estates at death: Nathan Mayer Rothschild died in Frankfurt on 28 July 1836; Ferguson puts his net worth at 0.62% of British national income. Natty, 1st Lord Rothschild, died on 31 March 1915 and Alfred succeeded him as senior partner. No probate figure for either estate was found.

entries.topic: The 1832 papal loan: the exclusivity clause

claims.text: Wikipedia gives the 1832 loan to the Holy See as £400,000 and mentions 'the original 5% contract, signed by Rothschild and Torlonia'.

The exclusivity clause (the Holy See could not approach another firm for a new loan without first informing the Rothschilds, who would get preference on equal terms) is footnoted on Wikipedia to Ignatius Balla, The Romance of the Rothschilds (1913), p. 229, a popular work, not to Ferguson. Ferguson appears only in that article's bibliography. No second source was found.
The Archive says the papal administration in Rome sought the Naples house's services and that five loans were issued between 1831 and 1850; it does not describe the terms.

Daniela Felisini's chapter 'The Pope's Banker' (Palgrave, 2016) describes the first Rothschild-Torlonia loan as made 'in partnership with James de Rothschild' and as 'one of the most controversial operations of the period', because of its financial conditions and because Rothschild was a Jewish banker. The abstract does not state the terms. Note: Felisini names James (Paris); Wikipedia names Carl (Naples).
